utterances.text: It is a crossroads of sorts. On one side, the road goes from Pristina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what is the issue and how does it arise from cross-examination? You are not at large. Re-examination does not provide an opportunity for you to lead evidence which you should have led in chief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, the thing is, and that was mentioned in cross-examination, that there was cooperation between the Verification Mission and the KLA, and I have a statement from William Walker. I questioned the witness about the importance of Malisevo, and he can say to what extent they discussed Malisevo with me. The subject, I repeat, was raised in cross-examination concerning the statements of this witness about the cooperation between the KVM, in general, and William Walker, in particular, on the one hand, and KLA, on the other. That is why I'm asking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's deal with it, then, as briefly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't have any recollection of this. Mr. Nice, can you help?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't have any recollection, but that's not to exclude the possibility that I may not have asked him questions about his possession of material on those topics in general terms. Because I frequently did. Given the paucity of contemporaneous material provided or the non-existence of such material, for the most part. Your Honours, while I'm on my feet, because I don't know if we'll be able to retrieve rapidly enough to make sensible use of time a passage where I did ask a question about this. Can I just return to the previous topic of the document produced, which indeed was provided by us. When I say it had a respectable source, so far as I can establish, it was provided to us by someone from the OSCE. Was it May of 1999? May of 1999, over the border in, I think, Macedonia. That, of course, says nothing about its being a genuine document in the hands of the person who handed it over. All I can say is that it's provided to us. There may be an OSCE official or an OSCE interpreter or translator was respectable. It doesn't say the document itself is or should be treated as genuine. If I'm able to find out more about the document and to make any concessions, I will, but otherwise it simply stands as a document that hasn't been explored.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Let's deal with this matter as briefly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The point here is the cooperation of William Walker with the KLA, and in his statement, he says, at the very beginning, something about a meeting with me, and he says: "Another issue had to do with --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm allowing you to put the question. What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, do you know what activities the KLA was engaged in Malisevo and what importance Malisevo held for the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Malisevo is in the centre of Drenica, an area which is generally known as a stronghold of the KLA, and they called Malisevo their capital town. It is important because it is on the Orahovac-Pristina road, and it is on the crossroad Malisevo-Blace-Orahovac, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since Malisevo is called the capital town of the KLA, how about the insistence of Walker, Holbrooke, and others to demilitarise it in any way linked with assistance lent to the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know when police -- when patrols followed the police on this road, it was always forbidden to go on with patrols on this road, because it was extremely dangerous. I know that because Dragobilje is one kilometre away from Malisevo, and that was the headquarters of the KLA. The police in Malisevo did not have the right to patrol around. They could only secure their own building. That was on the 2nd of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about this attention to Malisevo? Does it have anything to do with the assistance lent to the KLA headquarters and security given them?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is a section of the territory where only the verifiers had access. I could not -- or my units could not patrol there, because -- although it was my zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have another subject to cover with you. Both you and Mr. Nice, in relation to the event when a number of KLA members were killed near the border, you replayed that tape several times to see whether the captured people were KLA members and whether verifiers had access to them, and I remember Judge Bonomy asking to see the film again to see whether the verifiers actually spoke to the captured people. That remained unclear. In that connection, I have to ask you a couple of more questions, because I believe that is directly related to cross-examination and something that was contested in your statements. You spoke, General, of an incident that happened on the 14th December when a large group of terrorists, about 150 of them, clashed on the border with your patrol.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was on Pastrik Mountain, near the Likan watch-tower.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in relation to this incident you provided certain exhibits under tabs 212, 213, and 214, as well as a film, 216A?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the film. The rest of the exhibits constitute my analysis of what happened and a list of combat material that was seized then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was this the largest incident created by the KLA after the signing of the agreement concerning the verifiers?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 36 KLA were killed and nine were wounded. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were the verifiers notified and enabled to see the captured terrorists and talk to them?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said during my examination-in-chief. I said that General Drewienkiewicz said himself that the seized equipment had been viewed, but nobody had seen the captured terrorists. Only those that were killed. And I said that they were able to come to the spot. They even saw a clash, a bit of fighting that happened in their presence. They verified all the equipment. They verified and viewed the bodies. In one place, they saw the captured terrorists that were given assistance. As we could see on the video footage, they were able to get warm, near a fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We saw that on the video. Let me remind you only that General Drewienkiewicz said in his statement, page 16 in the Serbian version, said explicitly, describing this event: "But we never saw the prisoners, because we photographed the bodies and the equipment, but we never saw the captured terrorists." That is his claim. I asked you, however, to point us to the place in the video where we can see the prisoners, and you did that. Then during cross-examination, both Mr. Bonomy and Mr. Kwon asked you whether verifiers had talked to the prisoners, because we can see both parties on the video film, but we cannot see the conversation. Do you continue to claim that verifiers had unfettered access to the prisoners and talked to them?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, because I was present there all the time. And I stayed there even after they left, so that I could resolve the other questions that had to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know what the composition of the OSCE teams was, people who were present at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw two OSCE vehicles and I also saw these persons whom I had seen before. But as for their names, I don't know them. Most of my contacts were with General Mazenuv [phoen] and when he was absent, with his deputy. Lieutenant Colonel Mike Morrow, I think his name was. As for the others, my liaison officers talked to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. One of the members of that team, one of the members of that team is Ian Henry Roberts. I have his statement here, given on the 12th of October, 2000, the 15th of December, 2000, and the 17th of November, 2000. That's one of the verifiers who was there on the spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're waiting on the question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you remember that in General Drewienkiewicz's statements, he says that soldiers were not seen. Then it was challenged here that the verifiers could talk to these prisoners and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have to observe, of course, that before it leaves the screen, probably the critical question for the accused is the one he's already put in leading form, just going off towards the top of the page: "Do you continue to claim." I imagine that's what this is all about, but I'm not quite sure what detail the witness is actually giving of this or ever did. I understand we're well into the sixth hour of re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm finishing right now. I'm just going to read a quotation and then I'm going to put a question to General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So at the end of page 6 in the Serbian language, the ERN number is 03054577, he says: "The verifier, Ian Henry Roberts, he says they took us to the spot and showed it to us quite openly. It seemed that the dead people were there where they had fallen dead. I remember that about six soldiers of the KLA were taken prisoner. They were still on the spot and they allowed us access to those soldiers. We talked to them. We took their details. We even took pictures of them. One of the soldiers was wounded, and I think that later on he passed away. After a while, I think that the rest were released. I remember that we arrived early in the morning. The fighting took place the previous night. My impression was that members of the military and of the MUP --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Milosevic please be asked to slow down for the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you must put a question. I can't allow you to continue quoting from a passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So I read out a quotation to you from the statement of a member of the Verification Mission called Ian Henry Roberts, who was there on the spot and who says that they had access to prisoners, they talked to them, they took their details. Does this, General, corroborate everything that you asserted here during the cross-examination in this regard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are not a professionally trained advocate, and I don't know if that explains why you're not able to put questions without putting them in a leading manner. That's plainly leading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if a quotation from a statement made by the Verification Mission is leading, then my question is leading too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I tell you what you must do. You must cite that in your closing address or put it in your brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, first indeed it has to become evidence, and it can't really become evidence in this way through what is re-examination. However, since the name has been mentioned, and to tidy up the transcript at this stage, whatever happens to the statement of the man concerned, it's almost certainly not Ian Henry Roberts, but Ian Robert Hendrie, who the Chamber will remember is the witness who took the photographs at Racak, amongst other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I thought Mr. Milosevic was quoting from the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. He was quoting from a statement. But he has described it as the statement of someone called Ian Henry Roberts, but I'm pretty sure it's Ian Robert Hendrie, and we've heard him as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, do you have a question, a question that will be permissible, that satisfies our Rules of Procedure? If you don't, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, what about the members of the MUP and the army? Did they treat the dead as soldiers, not as terrorists, as far as this event is concerned?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a well-known principle which I think is observed in any army. As long as a man has a rifle and is fighting, he's the enemy. When he throws his rifle away, he becomes a prisoner. And when he's wounded, he's a wounded person. And once he is dead, he is a dead person who should be given all honours. And that is how my soldiers treated the dead enemy.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Milosevic please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the interpreters are asking you to slow down. And I'm now taking note, Mr. Milosevic, of the time you have spent in re-examination. And I'm going to consult my colleagues as to how much more time you should be given.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't need more than one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. You're going to end now. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ian Hendrie says: "Soldiers of the army of Yugoslavia treated the KLA dead with respect, and it seemed that they viewed them as soldiers, not terrorists or guerrillas. I also remember that the commander of the forces," that's you, right, "made an effort to show us everything."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I demand, Mr. Robinson, is to look at this statement. I read the Serbian version, but I have it in English too, and it has all kinds of signatures on it. I want that to be admitted, because it was challenged during the cross-examination that there were any conversations between the members of the Verification Mission and the KLA prisoners, although video footage was shown. And this is confirmation given by a KVM member who personally talked to them, who took pictures of them, took their details, and said all of that in his statement and signed that statement, at that. So I would like all of that to be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I've been taken by surprise by this, without any notice of the application that was going to be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you continue, as far as I remember, the witness has not answered any question on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He's been a witness already and hasn't been asked. This witness hasn't. But the statement is of a person who has already given evidence. This statement is of a person who has already given evidence in the trial and wasn't asked about it. Now, I'd like to know the legal basis for this statement now coming in, and that's what I was hoping that Mr. Kay could assist us with, because I can't think of it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I was trying to find the statement so that we could look at it and have a look and see what its terms were, which may be of interest. It may be a document that's agreed to go in with the Prosecution. I don't know. It just comes in as a document. We've got to have a look at it and see what it actually says, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are rules. There are ways of admitting written statements, and that's not been applied in relation to this statement, as far as I can see. And the opportunity was there to ask these questions when the witness gave evidence in the first place. So I don't see a legal basis at the moment for it, although it can no doubt happen by asking to bring the witness back or asking to present the statement in a form that complies with the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The other way, of course, is by agreement, which may be the case here, as it was a Prosecution witness statement. If it's not just being relied upon by one party under the legal mechanisms, which is what was going through my mind, it being a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the first part of what the speaker said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a Prosecution witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we know it's a Prosecution witness statement. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'd like to ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We just admitted three statements which was put to this witness by the Prosecution. I don't remember the names. What would be the base for admitting it, for you or for you to tender it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can't myself remember the names. I can't remember the names.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't remember those statements at the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. moment and I'll have to look into it. But there's a separate issue, and that is that circumstances in which you can admit statements in re-examination, and I respectfully adopt His Honour Judge Bonomy's point that there doesn't seem to be a mechanism that would allow for the production of this kind of statement at this stage and in this way. Before we move on, however, Ian Hendrie made a statement which was presented under 92 bis. It's Exhibit 214. We're trying to see whether that's the statement that is referred to. Because if it is, then that's the end of the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's only about the picture in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That was my guess. He came and he gave evidence. But if that statement doesn't cover it, then I'll need to have a look at the statement myself. I'll also need to review the precise scope of examination-in-chief and cross-examination, directed as I think it was at General Drewienkiewicz rather than at the others, but I'm not sure. And that his answers, rather than the answers of others, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Two matters arise. I think the statements that Judge Kwon is referring to were statements that weren't taken for the purposes of this trial, whereas the statement that we're looking at just now is a statement that was taken for the purpose of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The second point is the one Mr. Kay makes. If this is a Prosecution statement, then there may be a basis for agreeing that it should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There may be a basis for admitting it and it can be served, because no doubt it's the accused's desire to use the procedures of the Court under 89(F) or --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translations continues] ... to accord with our practices. But until I'm given a chance, and haven't so far, to examine this -- that's no criticism of the Chamber, of course. I'm referring to the circumstances and the manner of re-examination. Until I'm given a chance to look into it, I can't make a further position. But I'll do whatever I can to cooperate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll have to consider the matter. Mr. Milosevic, you wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Legal grounds are being questioned here. I'm leaving aside the fact that obviously what is the truth is playing second fiddle to what procedure is supposed to be. But what is being brought into question is General Delic's statement, namely, that the verifiers talked to the prisoners. Prisoners were seen in the video footage, but what was claimed was that it could not be seen that they were talking to the verifiers. But what we have here now is a statement of one of the verifiers, who confirms not only to have talked to the prisoners, but also he said that he took his -- took their details, took their pictures, et cetera. So this completely refutes what had been said, and I believe that that is sufficient grounds for admitting that into evidence. The statement was given in the year 2000 by a British verifier, the member of a Verification Mission. You have it here in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's like saying just because the Prosecution present a statement, then it must be true and reliable. What a ridiculous proposition to make. And, Mr. Milosevic, you fail to appreciate what the basic rules are in the presentation of evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You pick and choose your way through the statements and say: Well, if I like this one, it must be true and therefore it must be admissible. We can't proceed in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It sounds to me very much like a 92 bis application that we have here, and maybe we can attend to that and file it ourselves as a way of resolving the issue, unless the Prosecution wish to agree it, which would save a bit of paperwork.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: A certain passage of the statement was put to the witness, and the witness answered affirmatively. Is that not enough for the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't know. But he obviously wants the statement in for its entirety. We'll have to see how far it fits with 92 bis in terms of cumulative evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Admitted into evidence? What I ask to be admitted is what will confirm what General Delic says and challenge what Mr. Nice said. If necessary, I'm going to read out the whole thing in English, what it says here in this statement. I read it to the witness. The witness confirmed that that's the way it was. He was there on the spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have it under consideration, Mr. Milosevic, and we'll give our decision shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I raise one matter as the re-examination was ending?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just finish off with one question for General Delic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The matter is this: It's been very important to the accused's re-examination, the issue of the location of Lord Ashdown and whether matters should have been put by him in cross-examination concerning the visibility from Gegaj and a more detailed challenged to Lord Ashdown's position mounted. From my recollection of Lord Ashdown's first statement, i.e., the statement disclosed for the proceedings, I don't believe that Gegaj was mentioned as his place. The first mention of Gegaj comes about in his direct examination, his evidence in chief, when he mentions the place and he spells the name out for those listening. So the accused would not have been in a position to have mounted the kind of challenge in relation to the issue that he has had to mount in his own case. And in my submission, that has to be borne in mind and is a significant feature of the disclosure of all parties in this case relating to the evidence that they propose to call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because it was not mentioned, you say, in his first statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It was first mentioned during his examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He gave a description of events, but not a mention of the location, nor map coordinates, nor any of the issues that have come about in this trial. There was another feature of his evidence that in fact when he was being originally called by the Prosecution, Mr. Nice was going to deal with one matter only, and that was because Lord Ashdown's time was pressing, and that was to do with the menu and the Tudjman dinner. But somehow, we seamlessly moved from the menu and the Tudjman dinner into the full extent of his evidence, and he was available until lunch-time on the second day. He only gave evidence just over half a day. And the accused had to put his case in a very brief period of time and was reminded that time was brief, and he had to get on with matters, which again may have obviously -- would have affected the kinds of questions that he had to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That statement was admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Only one statement was admitted. There was a statement, which is Exhibit 81, which is a supplementary. The first page of that statement refers to an earlier interview, and I'm having difficulty finding that earlier interview and what manner of beast it was, what sort of disclosure document it was. And maybe the Prosecution can assist on that. But the exhibited statement is not the full statement. It was merely a clarification statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that has concluded the re-examination, there are some procedural issues that arise before the timetable for General Delic can be concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have concluded your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to ask one more question, Mr. Delic, with regard to a fact that he mentioned -- or rather he mentioned it and Mr. Nice mentioned it, that in 2002, the witness was engaged by Mr. Nice to establish a KLA crime. And in that respect, I have a question and want to say: Does that mean that when they engaged you, General, they had confidence in you and trusted you and they had no piece of information that would bring into question your credibility for the job?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You can't ask that. That is so leading. Thank you, Mr. Milosevic, for your re-examination, and thank you, Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The procedural issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We may have -- you're not to leave, of course. We have matters which may impinge ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I address you in private session, and indeed in the absence of the witness? Because some of the matters don't concern him or aren't available to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Before we go into private session, let's just resolve one matter out of the way concerning the Hendrie statement. It is in evidence already. Ms. Higgins has found it in Exhibit 214, the second statement, page 6 in the English, paragraph 35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that, Mr. Kay. That settles that. Thank you for your evidence, but you are not to leave the building. You may leave the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Some of it can be done in public session, if the Chamber would like, but I know that there's -- that the maximum amount should be dealt with in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, very well. And then we move to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as to public session, in light of the additional material provided by the accused that I imagine he's going to want exhibited, that's the maps and so on, in due course, I would seek to ask further questions of this witness, but I'm not in a position to do that immediately for reasons that I explained earlier today in private session. But given the way in which this issue has developed, the Chamber might think it would be desirable for the full potential evidential position of the Prosecution to be explored with this witness rather than simply to be left hanging. The second -- so that's one point. The second point, which I can deal with partly in public session and then I'll have to move to private session relates to a public filing by the Prosecution dated the 24th of August, the application for further action in relation to previous Rule 54 bis applications. The Chamber will recall that that application was based on the evidenced ease with which Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this witness had been able to find a range of documents that had been denied to the Prosecution. And the Court was urged to consider amending and expanding on its earlier orders, with particular regard to a schedule that was attached, detailing a range of documents that it might think it now appropriate to order or a further order to be produced. And indeed, the application focussed on documents that had been the subject not only of questions by the Prosecution but also questions by the Court, in particular, for example, issues in respect of -- or documents that might reveal the position about the joint command and documents that might reveal the full picture about Racak. If we can now go into, with Your Honours' leave, private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One matter of clarity. There were two documents put to General Delic during his testimony which involved printouts of the map from the video archives of the Tribunal. The Court may recollect that we produced those on the previous time that he was questioned, and Mr. Nice used them at that point, as well as with the text that had accompanied that part of the proceedings. In our submission, these should be made as exhibits, out of clarity, so that it is able to track what exactly was being put within the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's two documents. If they could be tab 1 and tab 2.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D311, tab 1 and tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I should say that Mr. Delic was consulted and -- let Mr. Delic be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before he comes in, I realise there was one other particular document I thought that I should refer to before the break. It's the rules of service of the VJ. You'll recall that he was asked questions about it, and it's clearly the accused's case that the legality of deployment of the army before the declaration of state of war is dependent on the legality of that document. Now, its legality or not, its legality, its force had been challenged. It's been referred to off and on in the evidence, as LiveNote shows. So far we haven't, and I've asked Mr. Kay for his assistance, neither of us can find it in our records as a produced exhibit. It only features as to its terms, so far as we know, in the thesis of this witness. And so we have a view on its constitutional position, which we've expressed in cross-examination, but it would be helpful if he's relying on that document, if he can provide us with a copy of it, and indeed of its legal source, or the source from which it derives, if it does, its authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And if it hasn't been produced as an exhibit, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It plainly should become an exhibit so that we can see its terms. I read the terms simply from the thesis, but I haven't, I think, seen the whole document. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The delay is explained by the fact that the witness who was scheduled to testify after Mr. Delic was being brought in. But now we have to have Mr. Delic in. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. If there's a problem finding Mr. Delic, then it might be as well to bring in Mr. Janicevic. Because Mr. Delic would be interposed for five minutes, for the purposes that we have in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can't hear Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're not getting any translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My microphone wasn't switched on. The family name Janicejevic is well known in Serbia, but the other family name, Janicevic, is also rather common. This witness is Janicevic, not Janicejevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it's my pronunciation you were correcting, but if it is, then I accept that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I heard the interpreters say Janicejevic. It's a common mistake because Janicejevic is actually more comment as a family name. Anyway, I wanted to make sure that everybody knows this witness's name is Janicevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General Delic, I understand that you're in agreement with the proposal that you stay on until next week, Wednesday, and indeed perhaps on Thursday as well, and maybe Friday. Hopefully not. Can you just confirm this for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If necessary, I will stay until next Wednesday or Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I commend you for your public spiritedness, Mr. Delic. Mr. Nice, with regard to the matters that may be subject to cross-examination by you, at this stage we can say that you'll be allowed to cross-examine on the VJ personnel files. The other matters in respect of which you have applied will be considered by the Chamber, and we'll give a decision shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, you may now leave. The attractions of The Hague are many, so I know your time will be well spent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting, Mr. Milosevic, you have Rules of Service with you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have the Rules with me, but I heard Mr. Delic saying to Mr. Nice yesterday, I believe, that he had sent him the Rules of Service two years ago. He sent his own copy that he had in his safe. So I don't have one, but I can get one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. Mr. Milosevic, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Janicevic, where were you born and when?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: 18th August 1951, in Berevce village, Strpce municipality, in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you constantly residing in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: From birth to 1999, I lived in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you complete your education and vocational training in Kosovo and Metohija as well?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: I finished primary school in Strpce high school in Kamenica, and the law school in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What jobs did you do?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: After I finished the school of the interior in Kamenica, I worked on a trial period until the 31st of December, 1971. From the 1st of January, 1972 until the 1st of July, 1992, I was a member of the SUP of Urosevac. I was a policeman then, inspector, commander of station, deputy commander of station, then again inspector. And from the 1st of July, 1992 I was elected at local elections for president of municipality in Strpce. I occupied that post until the 15th of June, 1995, when I was transferred again to the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia and appointed chief of SUP Urosevac. I remained in that office until the 15th of April, 1999, and from then on, until my retirement, I remained chief of Pristina SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: I'm currently a displaced person living in Nis. My family is in Strpce, in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you still in active service in the police force or are you retired?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: I retired on the 31st of December, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In what rank?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janicevic. Tell me: Since you were born in Kosovo, you lived and worked there almost all your life, tell me as briefly as you can about the inter-ethnic relations in Kosovo, especially in the municipality where you lived. I'm particularly interested in the period before the constitution of 1974 was adopted, and afterwards.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: Inter-ethnic relations in the entire Kosovo and Metohija, especially in my municipality, until 1968, until the first amendments to the constitution of the SFRY, were characterised by tolerance, and I can say they were good. After the amendments of 1968, and especially after the 1974 constitution was adopted, inter-ethnic relations starting deteriorating rapidly. All sorts of pressures began to be exerted by the province leadership that became independent then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was this deterioration like, and what were the tensions?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: They were expressed in the form of ethnic slurs, damage to farms, forests, theft of cattle, and other property and non-property-related forms of pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What you are describing now, was it characterised by some sort of discrimination against Serbs in Kosovo and Metohija? And do you have any knowledge about that discrimination in that period?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: Of course it was discriminatory. First of all, in the area of employment, proportionate representation principles were applied. If there were ten vacancies, one or two Serbs would be employed. In some cases, the ratio was 49:1. The criteria linked to actual skills were not observed, especially with regard to Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the situation in areas where Serbs were a majority?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: The principle of proportionate representation was applied everywhere, where Serbs were a majority, as well as in other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition in Strpce?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: 73 to 27, in favour of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was a large majority of Serbs, and the ratio of employment was still 1:7, 1:8.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the Assembly -- I'm not asking you about the Municipal Assembly. I'm asking you about the whole municipality as a territory.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, employment was guided by ethnic proportions. A proportionate number of Albanians were employed in all public services and institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean health, education, government?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the relevant time, were there physical attacks, murders?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were, in addition to ethnic slurs and provocations, there were also physical attacks, rapes. In that period, there were murders as well. There were two typical cases of murder, typical of the entire territory of Kosovo and Metohija. They happened in Vucitrn and Djakovica. Over the period of one month, there were two murders of Serbs on ethnic grounds, purely ethnic grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who was behind all that discrimination, tensions, rapes, murders?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: This violence was backed by nationalist, ethnic-based Albanian parties that were integrated at the time into the leadership of the province.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could we talk about a separatist movement there?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who were the targets of those separatist forces? Only Serbs or other non-Albanians as well?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: The targets were also Albanians, those Albanians who dared to stand up against that pressure and who tried to protect their Serb and other non-Albanian neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After the 1974 constitution, what attitude did the government of the province take towards such actions by the separatists?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: They were tolerant. In all such cases where Serbs or other non-Albanians were victimised, they were tolerant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the government agencies of the province or the Republic of Serbia -- you say the government of the province was tolerant, but did, for instance, the government of the Republic of Serbia try to do anything to protect that segment of the population?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: After the 1974 constitution, the organs of the Republic of Serbia could practically do nothing for the protection of the Serb and other non-Albanian population because the constitution prohibited any interference in the purview of the province. The province had its own assembly, its Executive Council, that is, the government, ministries or secretariats, that did all the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's leave Serbs aside for the moment. What was the attitude toward other ethnic communities, the Gorani, Turks, Romas, Turks [as interpreted] and others?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: That treatment was the same as the treatment of Serbs and Montenegrins, practically. They were different in another sense. They were openly assimilated over the past few years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of assimilation?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: In order for assimilation to be possible, in 1968 a law was enacted stipulating that the "ic" suffix was deleted from people's last name. For instance, Muratovic became Murati. So they became Albanised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say Muratovic, I suppose that person is a Muslim. But if you delete the suffix "ic" they lose any indication of their Serb origin and become treated as Albanian. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say they statistically became Albanians, did members of other ethnic communities, the Gorani, Roma, Turks and others, were they statistically translated, so to speak, into Albanians, in official documents?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. For instance, in the census of 1981, when the Albanians turned out for the regular census the last time, they would leave the column "nationality" empty, or they would pencil it in. The answer would be deleted and everybody would be registered as Albanian. Another example of pure assimilation was the opening of a school in the Albanian language in the Musnikovo village. That is near Strpce. Musnikovo is populated by Albanians and Serbs -- by Muslims and Serbs. Their mother tongue is Serb. They don't know Albanian, and still the school was in Albanian. After 1974, in order for people to get a job, they would have to write in their applications that they were Albanians, in 99 per cent of cases. For somebody to apply for a job and to get that job, they would have to fulfil the requirement of knowing Albanian. There are hundreds and thousands of similar examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, I hope that you have in front of you these binders with documents that accompany your testimony.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they were submitted to you. Could you open number 1. And now I'm asking you the following question: Is this a document of the Leskovac municipality dated the 18th of March, 2005?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please just read the first paragraph. We don't have to read out the names, all of them. What does it say here?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: It says here: "With reference to your request number 204-82-05 of the 15th of March, 2005, and pursuant to Article 61 of the law on registers of births, deaths, and marriages --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that the interpreters have a translation into English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Births, deaths and marriages, having inspected the registers which were restored, i.e., reconstructed in 1951, we notice that the following Serbs from Zaskok MK and Gatnje MK have been registered as being Siptar ethnicity, of Siptar ethnicity."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So when the registers in Leskovac were looked at again, this list of names was provided, obviously all of these names are Serb names?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just explain. The registers are in Leskovac at the moment. Otherwise, they are from Urosevac, or rather, from the village of Zaskok and the local commune of Gatnje, which is in the territory of the municipality of Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that. How did this happen? Do you have any explanation? Zaskok and Gatnje are hamlets. Are they predominantly Serb or Albanian?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: Mixed population, but the majority population is Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any explanation how come this happened? We can see the names and surnames of these persons and the names of their fathers. How were these persons registered as Albanians?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: The only explanation can be that even at that time, the Albanians were trying to act in an inappropriate manner in their wish to increase the Albanian population in Kosovo. I don't have this kind of document here now, but in practically all the municipalities in Kosovo and Metohija, even church land was registered as being the property of the Islamic religious community, or simply as village land. There is no other explanation. I'm sorry. If this were a mistake, a mere error, a single one would be made, not in 30 or 50 places.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These are 25 names from these two villages only?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I'm asking for this to be admitted into evidence. This is an official document of the municipal administration for general affairs in Leskovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Signed and stamped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: A number for the binder.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D312, for two binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it two or four binders? Four binders, but we only have two. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask a question? Your evidence so far has been that until 1968, everything was fine. How do you account for these changes being made in the 1960s and 1950s to the register?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say everything was fine until 1968. There were cases of such attempts against Serbs and Montenegrins and their integrity, but they were much rarer before 1968.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your answer was: "Inter-ethnic --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Bonomy, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your answer was that: "Inter-ethnic relations in the entire Kosovo and Metohija, especially in your municipality, until 1968, were characterised by tolerance, and I can say they were good."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what I'm saying now too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this document has nothing to do with inter-ethnic relations. This document has to do with administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what's the point you're making about administration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said a few minutes ago that nationalist separatists got into the state structures in Kosovo and Metohija, government agencies, and that through persons employed there, they tried in a way to attain their objectives and to carry out their ideas. That's what they did and that's what they're doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that was happening in 1957?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And indeed 1954. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if the Court is rising at its normal time today. There's just literally 30 seconds I want to mention in private session, nothing to do with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Another question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, we've just seen this document. What about these persons mentioned here and what was established when the registers were being re-established? Do these persons know that somebody had registered them as Albanians?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: No. Until the 1960s, no one had any idea of them being registered as Albanians in the registers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's because the registers were kept by Albanians; right?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These tensions and what was going on in terms of what you've described so far, did all of this affect the Serbs in Kosovo and Metohija? Did they leave Kosovo and Metohija because of that? Or, to the best of your knowledge, when did Serbs start moving out at a faster rate or a more intensive rate from Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: Serbs and Montenegrins started leaving Kosovo and Metohija at a more intensive pace as of 1974, when the new constitution was adopted. After the hostile demonstrations in 1981, the numbers only went up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before you tell me something about these demonstrations, were Turks moving out, Muslims, Gorani, and others?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC
utterances.text: All non-Albanians were moving out, all of those who felt threatened by their Albanian neighbours. The Gorani were leaving and going to Turkey, then the Turks, the Romany, they were leaving too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janicevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, you said one more question, so I put that additional question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Possibly in private session, if you'd be so good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nothing to do with this witness, but he can stay. I'm not concerned -- well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You won't be very long?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now until tomorrow, 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 22nd day of September, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
